ruststream-kinesis 的位置：在 RustStream 运行时与 AWS SDK 之间，每个分片一个读取者，旁边是租约存储，每个运行时一个 SDK 客户端。
Kinesis 流是一组分片，每个分片都是一个有序的记录日志，每个消费者都各自读取每个分片，直到保留期结束。
服务的各个实例通过租约表共享一个流的分片：每个分片一行，记录它的所有者、到期时间和检查点。
消费者用迭代器读取分片：GetShardIterator 把迭代器放到分片的日志上，每次 GetRecords 返回记录和下一个迭代器。
一个分片承担流吞吐量中固定的一份；拆分或合并会关闭分片并打开子分片，子分片在其父分片之后读取。
一个订阅为每个分片使用一个读取者，通过一个通道读取它的分片；workers(n, by_key) 把记录分到按分区键划分的工作分区上。
KinesisBroker::new 只记录配置，connect 加载 AWS 配置，每个订阅打开它的分片，shutdown 关闭连接。
一条 Kinesis 记录在 RustStream 服务中的路径：读取、投递、处理器、应答和检查点，逐条进行或按批进行。
ack、drop、retry 和 retry_after 在 Kinesis 上变成什么；Kinesis 为每个分片保存一个检查点，而不是逐条确认记录。
The parts of ruststream-kinesis a Kinesis service uses, one page per component.
With asyncapi the document speaks Kinesis: the server's host, and an x-ruststream-kinesis object on each channel and keyed message.
A subscription's channel reports its stream, read pause and provisioned shards; a publishing position's channel reports the stream it writes.
A policy with a partition key reports it on the message object, since a key routes one record and names no stream.
The server reports the endpoint's host and port with the protocol kinesis, the regional host when a region is named, and never a credential.
KinesisBroker connects a service to Kinesis Data Streams; new records configuration only, and the runtime builds the SDK client at startup.
Credentials and region resolve through the AWS default chain at connect; from_config takes a prebuilt SdkConfig, which a DynamoDB lease store shares.
endpoint, region and test_credentials point the broker at a local stack such as LocalStack; each overrides one setting of the default chain.
KinesisError is the crate's one error type: stream admin, reads, aggregated records, publishes, leases, a closed connection and invalid descriptors.
One glob, ruststream_kinesis::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, the descriptor, positions, context keys and the publish surface.
Shutdown closes the connection; a publisher or a seek handle taken earlier reports KinesisError::NotConnected instead of acting.
A subscription opens once every shard it took has a reader and a starting cursor; a stream the service lacks fails startup unless the descriptor creates it.
Context<'_, KinesisContext> gives a handler the record's position and the seek handle, through the Position and SeekHandle keys.
A batch handler's context carries only the seek handle, so asking for a record's position in a batch body does not compile.
User headers ride an RSK2 envelope in front of the payload, only when there are any; a record from another producer reads as headerless.
Every delivery carries its sequence number, its shard and its partition key as headers, where the framework's per-key dispatch finds the key.
A lease store holds each shard's owner and checkpoint: acquire, renew, checkpoint, read and release, with SHARD_END marking a finished shard.
DynamoLeaseStore keeps leases in a DynamoDB table, so several instances share the shards; the table needs only a string key lease_key.
LeaseKey names one shard of one stream; a store of your own keys its rows by the key's stream:shard form.
legacy_stream names the stream a table's bare shard rows belong to, so a table written by an earlier version resumes from them.
MemoryLeaseStore is the default store: correct for one service instance, and empty again after a restart.
owner_id names this instance in the lease table; left out, each broker takes an id of its own, unique to that broker.
KinesisPosition names a place in the stream: the trim horizon, the tip, an arrival timestamp on every shard, or one record of one shard.
A handler moves its running subscription through the SeekHandle key; a sequence position moves one shard, the others move every shard.
start_at opens the subscription at a position you name on every startup, ahead of the stored checkpoints.
KinesisPublish, Publish in the prelude, writes each record with one PutRecord; it is the broker's default, so a reply needs no policy.
A record's partition key picks its shard and its order; four places can name it, and a record nobody keyed gets a process-unique one.
The partition_key step keys one record on the publish builder; a body that names it bounds its slot on KinesisPublishOptions.
partition_key at the mount site keys every record of a position, a reply included, which has no publish call to put a step on.
An ack is a per-shard checkpoint: it moves only when every earlier record is handled; drop retires a record, and a requeue is unsupported.
max_attempts caps deliveries per record; dead_letter names the stream a spent record leaves for, and a cap without one retires the record.
out_retry replaces the publisher the retry copies leave through, so the copies take a transform or a codec of the mount site's choosing.
retry_after publishes a copy of the record back to its stream once the delay is over, with the attempt count in a header; the copy arrives at the tip.
A stream name in #[subscriber] reads every shard of that stream; KinesisStream carries every other setting of the subscription.
A slice handler gets up to batch(n) records; n becomes the GetRecords limit, and a short batch goes out 50 ms after its first record.
create_if_missing creates the stream with the shard count it names when it is missing, then waits up to a minute for it to become active.
KinesisStream describes one subscription by stream name, with its read pause and the shards it provisions when the stream is missing.
poll_interval sets the pause between reads of an idle shard, one second by default; the service allows five reads a second per shard.
A subscription lists shards every ten seconds, leases each one, reads it with one reader, and starts a split's children after their parents.
KinesisSubscriberExt puts poll_interval and create_if_missing on the mount chain, after batch(n) and before start_at(..).

ruststream-kinesis 如何测量自己：三个循环、在 Kinesis 端点上的运行、受模拟器限制的判定计算，以及代码计数。流程就是框架自己的流程（RustStream 方法论），本页说明它在 Kinesis 上是什么样子。

一个进程把每个场景跑三遍，作为三个循环，它们只有一处不同：承载记录的是什么。 裸客户端。 直接驱动 aws-sdk-kinesis：在分片迭代器上调用 GetRecords，解码每条记录，为它写入检查点，并按本 crate 的节奏续约。 Broker crate。 本 crate，上面什么也没有：Broker 建立连接，KinesisStream 描述符打开一个订阅，一个循环从它的流中取出投递、解码并 ack。 RustStream。 用户写的服务：一个 #[subscriber] 处理器及其外围的应用。 其余一切在三个循环中都相同：同一个 SdkConfig 构建所有客户端，流只有一个分片，每次读取请求 1,000 条记录，空读取等待 20 毫秒，检查点写到同样的地方，解码成同一个结构体，载荷字节、带四个工作线程的 tokio 运行时，以及二进制程序。这个等待时间有意远低于默认的一秒：回环接口上的模拟器没有按分片计算的读取额度，一秒的休眠只会测出休眠本身。 消息体是 512 字节的 JSON。它解码成一个包含两个整数字段的结构体，因此解码不做内存分配，数字反映的是本 crate，而不是 JSON 解析器。

每次运行使用新的流。 每次运行创建自己的单分片流，DynamoDB 场景还创建自己的租约表，因此一次运行永远看不到之前的运行留下的东西。 消费者先接入，从 trim horizon 开始读取。随后十六个任务填充流，每条记录一次 PutRecord，并且最多领先消费者 50,000 条记录。 在三个循环中，计时窗口都从第一次投递开始，到读出最后一条记录的字段时结束。 创建流、获取租约和打开迭代器都在窗口之外。 记录条数来自一次探测，它测量裸循环的速率，因此在任何机器上，测量的运行都至少持续五秒。 各循环交替进行：裸、crate、RustStream，共三轮。每个循环报告它最佳、中位和最差的一轮。 当与端点之间的往返至少占一次投递所用时间的一半时，该行标为 受模拟器限制。这是算出来的。在发布任何记录之前，一次探测用一个独立的客户端，为端点能应答的最小请求 DescribeStreamSummary 计时。一次投递分摊承载它的那次 GetRecords 调用的一份，在 DynamoDB 场景下还要加上结算它的那次条件写入。文档按行把这份分摊公布为 round_trips_per_message。往返时间乘以这份分摊达到每条记录测得时间的一半时，该行就被标记。往返时间与机器信息一起公布，因此这个计算可以核对。

开销图的每个场景都是用户写的服务，基于 KinesisBroker，连接同一个端点，构建时不带 testing 特性，在单线程运行时上启动。它从 trim horizon 读取一个为本次运行创建的单分片流，并通过默认的租约存储写入检查点。另一个线程在测量区间打开之前填充流，这个线程不计入。 指令数来自 callgrind，内存分配来自 DHAT。一个场景依次在一次投递、1000 次、2000 次上运行。后两次之差是一条记录的稳态开销，单次投递就是冷启动。一次读取由它返回的记录分摊，因此每一行都带有一次读取的一份：前两行每次读取最多一千条记录，第三行是一个 64 条记录的批。 计数涵盖服务线程运行的一切：运行时、本 crate，以及 AWS SDK 及其 HTTP 栈。SDK 自己运行的线程不计入，往返中端点那一侧的工作也不计入。同一构建的各次运行之间，指令数的变动小于百分之零点五，因为服务做真实的 I/O：一次排空结束时可能还有一次读取在途，续约和分片列举也由计时器触发。与保存的基线对照时，某个场景的指令数多出百分之二就算失败。内存分配在每次运行中都受每个场景声明的下限约束，下限高于观测到的最大计数。

同一行中的三个循环可以互相比较，因为它们在同一个进程中、交替地、对着同一个端点运行。一行不能与另一个 Broker crate 公布的行比较：各种传输在每条记录上做的工作不同。 一次读取承载最多一千条记录，因此它分摊到一条记录上的份额很小。在 DynamoDB 那一行，每条记录还要付出一次属于自己的条件写入，即它的 ack 背后的检查点。在 受模拟器限制 的行中，往返至少占了一次投递所用时间的一半。本 crate 和运行时的工作于是发生在一段裸客户端同样要付出的等待之内，各循环之间的差异是这部分工作的下界，而不是对它的测量。 决定两行节奏的，是模拟器在一个分片上接收和返回记录的速度，与哪个循环读取它们无关，而往返计算不统计这一点。因此一行中的三个循环都落在彼此的波动范围之内。这两行说明，本 crate 和运行时都没有高出这个下限。它们没有说明在更快的测试环境上三者会如何比较。

指令计数包含运行时、本 crate，以及 AWS SDK 在服务线程上的工作：构建并签名每个请求、HTTP 交换，以及解析每个应答。一次投递分摊一次 GetRecords 的一份，应答还要加上一次属于自己的 PutRecord，所以应答那一行几乎全是 SDK 的工作。每个数字的大部分都是 SDK 的工作，而不是本 crate 的工作，这些数字不能与客户端在自己线程上工作的 Broker 的数字相比。同样的计数在缓存未命中处要花更多时间，因此计数不等于时间。 每个数字都是稳态，即 1000 次投递的运行与 2000 次投递的运行之差。连接、打开订阅、列出分片、获取它的租约和迭代器，以及它们背后的首批内存分配属于冷启动，只付一次。

测试环境是 LocalStack，一个 Kinesis 和 DynamoDB 的模拟器，而不是托管服务。它在回环接口上用普通 HTTP 应答，没有 TLS 握手、凭证刷新和区域的延迟。对照仍然成立，因为三个循环都与同一个模拟器通信。吞吐量不能推及真实服务：区域中的流有按分片计算的限制，应答的时间尺度也不同。 一行就是一个分片、一个消费者和 512 字节的消息体。它测量的是一条记录在本 crate 内部的开销，而不是 Kinesis 能承载多少。 在三个循环中，计时窗口都在读出最后一条记录的字段时、在写入它的检查点之前关闭，因此每次运行都有一个检查点处于所有数字之外。追上填充者的消费者在空读取之后要付出 20 毫秒的等待，这段等待计入被它推迟的那条记录。 这些数字是一台机器在某一天的快照，构建信息记录在旁边。它们在一台只做这次运行的机器上手动重新测量：它们显示的差异小于共享机器的噪声。

服务的各个实例通过租约表共享一个流的分片：每个分片一行，记录它的所有者、到期时间和检查点。 两个实例通过租约表共享一个流的分片，一个实例的租约失效时，另一个实例接管它的分片每 3 秒续约每 3 秒续约租约表实例 A持有分片 0orders:shardId-000000000000所有者 A、到期时间、计数器、检查点orders:shardId-000000000001所有者 B、到期时间、计数器、检查点实例 B持有分片 1A 停止后，它的租约在 10 秒后失效。B 用条件写入接管这一行，并从 A 写入的检查点之后继续读取 以文字阅读本图 租约表: orders:shardId-000000000000 所有者 A、到期时间、计数器、检查点; orders:shardId-000000000001 所有者 B、到期时间、计数器、检查点 实例 A 持有分片 0 → orders:shardId-000000000000 所有者 A、到期时间、计数器、检查点: 每 3 秒续约 实例 B 持有分片 1 → orders:shardId-000000000001 所有者 B、到期时间、计数器、检查点: 每 3 秒续约 A 停止后，它的租约在 10 秒后失效。B 用条件写入 接管这一行，并从 A 写入的检查点之后 继续读取 Kinesis 不记录谁在读取某个分片，也不记录读到了哪里。Kinesis Client Library 把这些信息保存在一张 DynamoDB 表中，每个分片一行，它的工作进程会接管无人续约的行。本 crate 通过 LeaseStore 做同样的事。存储可以为某个所有者获取分片、续约、记录检查点、读取一行以及释放它。每一行都以流和分片共同作为键，因为分片 id 在不同的流之间会重复。 租约持续 10 秒，它的读取者每 3 秒续约一次。续约失败的读取者已经把分片让给了另一个所有者，它立即停止，不写入检查点。新的所有者从最后一个检查点开始读取，因此少数记录可能被投递两次。投递是至少一次的。 DynamoLeaseStore 由 dynamodb-lease 特性启用，它把这些行保存在一张 DynamoDB 表中。该表只有一个字符串键 lease_key，写作 stream:shard。一行包含 lease_owner、lease_expiry、lease_counter 和 checkpoint。每次写入都是条件写入。当这一行没有所有者、所有者就是自己，或者租约已经过期时，获取成功。续约、检查点和释放只在本所有者持有这一行时成功。读取是强一致的。每个 Broker 都有自己的租约所有者 id，默认唯一，因此两个实例绝不会同时持有一个分片。 MemoryLeaseStore 是默认的存储。它存在于进程中：对单个实例是正确的，重启后又变为空。于是重启后的服务没有检查点，每个分片都从最新处打开，除非 start_at(..) 指定了另一个位置。 存储属于一个 Broker。一个 Broker 通过一个订阅读取一个流，对同一个流的第二个订阅会在启动时被拒绝。两个各有自己租约存储的 Broker，无论位于一个服务中还是两个服务中，都各自读取整个流。共用一张表的实例共享分片。 这一模型就是 Kinesis Client Library 的租约表（KCL 消费者），加上 DynamoDB 的条件写入（条件表达式）。

一个分片承担流吞吐量中固定的一份；拆分或合并会关闭分片并打开子分片，子分片在其父分片之后读取。 拆分把分片 0 变为分片 1 和 2，合并把分片 1 和 2 变为分片 3，每个子分片都在其父分片之后读取拆分拆分合并合并分片 0，已关闭有结束序列号分片 1，已关闭0 的下半段分片 2，已关闭0 的上半段分片 3，打开父分片 1 和 2每个父分片都读到末尾之后，才读取子分片，因此同一个键的记录在变更前后保持顺序 以文字阅读本图 分片 0，已关闭 有结束序列号 → 分片 1，已关闭 0 的下半段: 拆分 分片 0，已关闭 有结束序列号 → 分片 2，已关闭 0 的上半段: 拆分 分片 1，已关闭 0 的下半段 → 分片 3，打开 父分片 1 和 2: 合并 分片 2，已关闭 0 的上半段 → 分片 3，打开 父分片 1 和 2: 合并 每个父分片都读到末尾之后，才读取子分片， 因此同一个键的记录在变更前后 保持顺序 每个分片每秒最多接受 1 MB 或 1,000 条记录的写入。它每秒最多提供 2 MB 的读取，并且每秒最多接受五次 GetRecords 调用。读取该分片的所有消费者共用这五次调用，因此这一限制与计费无关：它决定分片究竟能被读取多频繁。预置模式的流拥有为它分配的分片，按需模式的流按流量需要获得分片。 拆分把一个分片的哈希键范围分给两个子分片。合并把两个相邻的分片合为一个。无论哪种方式，父分片都会关闭：ListShards 为它们报告一个结束序列号，它们不再接受新记录，已有的记录保留到保留期结束。读到已关闭分片末尾的读取者拿不到下一个迭代器：这就是 SHARD_END。 同一个键的记录可能先位于父分片上，之后位于子分片上。为了保持它们的顺序，消费者先把每个父分片读到末尾，再读取子分片。本 crate 在获取每个子分片的租约之前检查这一点：每个父分片都必须在租约存储中标为 SHARD_END，或者已因保留期裁剪而从列表中消失。订阅从最新处开始时，没有检查点的已关闭父分片算作已读完，因为它的旧记录反正会被跳过。读取者只在其分片的每次投递都结算之后，才写入 SHARD_END。 订阅每 10 秒重新列出一次分片，因此父分片读完后，子分片会在这段时间内打开。子分片的读取者从子分片的检查点继续读取，读取一页用图说明了这一点。没有检查点的子分片从它最旧的记录打开，因此在读取者启动之前写入子分片的记录也会被读到。create_if_missing(shards) 以预置模式创建缺失的流，分片数为指定的数量，并最多等待一分钟，直到流可用。 这一模型就是 Amazon Kinesis Data Streams 自己的模型（配额和限制、容量模式、重新分片、重新分片之后的读取）。

The parts of ruststream-kinesis a Kinesis service uses, one page per component: the broker (KinesisBroker), its stream subscriptions, its checkpoints and lease stores, its positions, its publish policy and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on. The crate reads and writes Amazon Kinesis Data Streams through the official aws-sdk-kinesis client. On top of the client it finds a stream's shards, leases each shard to one instance of the service and keeps a checkpoint per shard. A service adds ruststream-kinesis = "0.7" to its dependencies, beside the framework itself. Three cargo features are off by default and only add to the crate. dynamodb-lease adds DynamoLeaseStore, so several instances of a service share the shards. asyncapi adds the Kinesis objects of the generated AsyncAPI document. testing adds the in-process mode a TestApp test connects.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks Kinesis: the server's host, and an x-ruststream-kinesis object on each channel and keyed message. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. The specification defines no Kinesis binding, and its list of binding keys is closed. So this crate writes its own objects under the extension key x-ruststream-kinesis. A server reports the host clients connect to. A channel reports the stream behind it, and a subscription's channel its read settings too. A message reports the partition key the mount site fixed. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors and the policies. The document is built without a connection, so an existing stream's real shard count is not in it. The document is published and shared, so it carries no credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-kinesis = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label kinesis, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example kinesis_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { // The label is the server's key in the document. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled("kinesis", broker, |b| { // Every receipt carries one key, so they share a shard and keep their order. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("tenant-acme"); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker()) } examples/manual/kinesis_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { // The label is the server's key in the document. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled("kinesis", broker, |b| { // Every receipt carries one key, so they share a shard and keep their order. b.include(subscriber(orders(), Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("tenant-acme"); }) } fn app() -> impl App { service(broker()) }

A subscription's channel reports its stream, read pause and provisioned shards; a publishing position's channel reports the stream it writes. A KinesisStream writes three fields into its channel's x-ruststream-kinesis object. stream is the stream it reads, and pollIntervalMs the pause between reads of an idle shard, in milliseconds. shardCount is the number of shards create_if_missing gives the stream, and it is there only when the descriptor creates the stream. A channel the service publishes to reports stream, the stream its records land in. The policy holds no destination, so the stream is the one the mount site resolved: a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], a reply("stream") clause, or the name of a slot entry.

The subscription reads orders every quarter of a second and creates it with two shards, and its replies land in receipts. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_asyncapi.rs /// Reads `orders` every quarter of a second, and creates it with two shards where it is missing. #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("orders") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(2), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { id: order.id } } examples/manual/kinesis_asyncapi.rs /// Confirms each order with a receipt. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { id: order.id })) } } /// Reads `orders` every quarter of a second, and creates it with two shards where it is missing. fn orders() -> KinesisStream { KinesisStream::new("orders") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(2) } The channel orders in the document: tests/snippets/asyncapi-channel.json { "x-ruststream-kinesis": { "pollIntervalMs": 250, "shardCount": 2, "stream": "orders" } } The channel receipts: tests/snippets/asyncapi-publish-channel.json { "x-ruststream-kinesis": { "stream": "receipts" } }

A policy with a partition key reports it on the message object, since a key routes one record and names no stream. A key named on the policy with KinesisPublishSettings applies to every record that leaves through it. So the message object of those records carries it as partitionKey in its x-ruststream-kinesis object. The stream stays on the channel: one message type published to two streams describes both with one message object. A policy with no key adds no object to the message. A key named on one publish with the partition_key step describes one record, not the mount, so it is not in the document.

The receipts leave through a policy keyed tenant-acme. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { // The label is the server's key in the document. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled("kinesis", broker, |b| { // Every receipt carries one key, so they share a shard and keep their order. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("tenant-acme"); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { // The label is the server's key in the document. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled("kinesis", broker, |b| { // Every receipt carries one key, so they share a shard and keep their order. b.include(subscriber(orders(), Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("tenant-acme"); }) } The message object of Receipt in the document: tests/snippets/asyncapi-message.json { "x-ruststream-kinesis": { "partitionKey": "tenant-acme" } }

The server reports the endpoint's host and port with the protocol kinesis, the regional host when a region is named, and never a credential. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its protocol is kinesis, and its host comes from the first of these that applies: a broker with an endpoint reports that URL's host and port; the scheme and any user name and password stay out; a broker with a region reports that region's host, kinesis.<region>.amazonaws.com; any other broker reports kinesis.amazonaws.com, because its region resolves from the environment only when it connects. The host comes from the broker's own steps. A broker built with from_config connects where its config points and reports a host from its steps all the same.

The broker runs in eu-west-1, and the document reports kinesis.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_asyncapi.rs /// The broker in `eu-west-1`, whose regional endpoint the document reports. fn broker() -> KinesisBroker { KinesisBroker::new().region("eu-west-1") } examples/manual/kinesis_asyncapi.rs /// The broker in `eu-west-1`, whose regional endpoint the document reports. fn broker() -> KinesisBroker { KinesisBroker::new().region("eu-west-1") }

KinesisBroker connects a service to Kinesis Data Streams; new records configuration only, and the runtime builds the SDK client at startup. KinesisBroker::new() does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: the AWS credentials and region, a local endpoint, and the lease store and owner id that let several instances share the shards. A setting the service leaves out comes from the AWS SDK's default chain. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedKinesisBroker. The connect loads the AWS configuration and builds the SDK client; it sends no request to Kinesis. Every subscription and every publisher of the service runs on that connected form, and the first requests go out when the subscriptions start. A handler that runs on a thread of its own publishes and checkpoints through a client built for that thread from the same configuration, so one busy runtime never holds up another's requests. At shutdown the runtime consumes the connected form, and the connection is closed. #[subscriber("orders")] reads every shard of the stream orders. The descriptor KinesisStream carries the settings of a subscription, and the Subscriptions pages describe them. Records leave through the KinesisPublish policy, the broker's default.

The service reads the stream orders. The region and the credentials come from the environment it runs in. cargo run --example kinesis_service --features testing -- run starts it. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_service.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// Reads every shard of the stream `orders`. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_service.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// Reads every shard of the stream `orders`. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Place).build()); }) }

Credentials and the region resolve through the AWS SDK's default chain at connect; from_config takes a prebuilt SdkConfig, which a DynamoDB lease store shares. A broker built with new loads its configuration with aws_config when the runtime connects it. The region comes from AWS_REGION or the shared profile. The credentials come from the environment, the shared profile files, SSO, or the instance or container role. The SDK fetches them on the first request, a subscription's DescribeStreamSummary at startup, so a service with a subscription meets a missing credential there. The configuration follows the SDK's latest behaviour version. from_config takes an aws_config::SdkConfig the service builds itself: a named profile, a pinned behaviour version, its own HTTP client or credential provider. The broker uses that config as it is. The region, the credentials and the endpoint all come from it, and the broker's own endpoint, region and test_credentials steps do not apply. A DynamoLeaseStore is built from an SdkConfig too, so a service that uses one hands the same config to both. Transport security is the SDK's HTTPS client in both cases. The service's role needs these permissions: Action When kinesis:DescribeStreamSummary, kinesis:ListShards, kinesis:GetShardIterator, kinesis:GetRecords every subscription kinesis:CreateStream, kinesis:DescribeStream a subscription with create_if_missing kinesis:PutRecord every publish dynamodb:GetItem, dynamodb:UpdateItem a DynamoLeaseStore, on its table

The service signs its requests with the orders profile of the shared AWS files, in eu-west-1. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_credentials.rs /// The credentials of the `orders` profile in the shared AWS files, in `eu-west-1`. The broker /// uses the config as it is. fn config() -> SdkConfig { let profile = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::latest()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(profile)) .build() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(KinesisBroker::from_config(config())) } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_credentials.rs /// The credentials of the `orders` profile in the shared AWS files, in `eu-west-1`. The broker /// uses the config as it is. fn config() -> SdkConfig { let profile = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::latest()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(profile)) .build() } fn app() -> impl App { service(KinesisBroker::from_config(config())) }

endpoint, region and test_credentials point the broker at a local stack such as LocalStack; each overrides one setting of the default chain. endpoint replaces the AWS endpoint with an address such as http://localhost:4566, where LocalStack listens. region sets the region every request is signed for. test_credentials signs requests with a fixed dummy key: a local stack checks that a request is signed and ignores the key. Each step overrides only its own setting, and the SDK's default chain resolves the rest. The three steps apply to a broker built with new; a broker built with from_config takes all three from its config. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the endpoint's host and port as the server. A broker with no endpoint and a named region is reported as that region's Kinesis host, kinesis.<region>.amazonaws.com.

The service runs against a local stack on port 4566. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_endpoint.rs /// The broker on the local stack at `endpoint`: the region is named, and the credentials are /// dummies the stack accepts. fn broker(endpoint: &str) -> KinesisBroker { KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("http://localhost:4566")) } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_endpoint.rs /// The broker on the local stack at `endpoint`: the region is named, and the credentials are /// dummies the stack accepts. fn broker(endpoint: &str) -> KinesisBroker { KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials() } fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("http://localhost:4566")) }

KinesisError is the crate's one error type: stream admin, reads, aggregated records, publishes, leases, a closed connection and invalid descriptors. Each variant names the step that failed, and most also name the stream and the shard. The SDK error behind it is its source, formatted with its whole cause chain, so the SDK's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Stream the stream is missing, or describing or creating it failed Read listing the shards, opening an iterator or reading records failed, or a seek named a shard this instance does not read AggregatedRecord a record was written by the Kinesis Producer Library's aggregation, which the crate does not unpack Publish the service refused a record or did not store it Lease the lease store failed, or refused a row it cannot read NotConnected a publisher or a seek handle was used after the broker shut down Invalid the descriptor cannot work, such as an empty stream name or a shard count below one A service meets the error in three places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. A failure while a subscription runs, such as a read that keeps failing, is logged by the runtime as an error that names the stream and the shard. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

An archive record the service refuses is logged with its cause, and the invoice is settled as a retry. The mount site caps the retries at three deliveries, and then the invoice leaves for invoices.unarchived. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_errors.rs /// Archives each invoice under its customer's reference, so one customer's invoices stay in /// order. A record the service refuses is logged with its cause and retried; the mount site caps /// the retries. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("invoices"))] async fn archive( invoice: &Invoice, Out(archives): Out<impl Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>, Archive>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let sent = archives .message(&Archived { invoice: invoice.id, }) .partition_key(invoice.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { // The error names the stream and the service's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "invoices", invoice.id, error = %err, "archive refused"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_errors.rs /// Archives each invoice under its customer's reference, so one customer's invoices stay in /// order. A record the service refuses is logged with its cause and retried; the mount site caps /// the retries. struct File; impl<Entry> Handle<Invoice, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for File where Entry: OutEntry<Archive, Wire: Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let sent = outs .get(Archive) .message(&Archived { invoice: invoice.id, }) .partition_key(invoice.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { // The error names the stream and the service's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "invoices", invoice.id, error = %err, "archive refused"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

One glob, ruststream_kinesis::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, the descriptor, positions, context keys and the publish surface. use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; is the one import a Kinesis service writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds KinesisBroker, the descriptor KinesisStream with its mount-site steps KinesisSubscriberExt, and KinesisPosition with the core's Seeker and Positioned. It adds the contexts KinesisContext and KinesisBatchContext with their keys Position and SeekHandle, and the seeker type KinesisSeeker. With the dynamodb-lease feature it adds DynamoLeaseStore. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is KinesisPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on that name; the prefixed type at the crate root tells them apart. The prelude also brings KinesisPublishSettings, KinesisPublishSteps and KinesisPublishOptions. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher, Slot>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that names a record's partition key: it needs KinesisPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>, Slot>, both from this prelude.

The descriptor, its read pause, the start position, the context key and the reply policy with its key all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("orders").poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)), start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, position = ?at, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts-v1"); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// Confirms each order with a receipt, and logs where the order sits in the stream. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), KinesisContext> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, position = ?ctx.context(Position), "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { let orders = KinesisStream::new("orders").poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)); b.include( subscriber(orders, Confirm) .reply() .build() .start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts-v1"); }) }

Shutdown closes the connection; a publisher or a seek handle taken earlier reports KinesisError::NotConnected instead of acting. At shutdown the runtime stops the subscriptions first. Each shard reader then releases its lease, so another instance can take the shard at once instead of waiting for the lease to expire. A publish is one PutRecord call that returns when the service has stored the record, so the broker holds no queue to flush. Then the runtime shuts the broker down. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. KinesisBroker::publisher hands one out before the service starts, for code that publishes outside any handler. It shares the broker's connection, so it publishes once the service is up. After the shutdown a publish through it returns KinesisError::NotConnected, and never writes to a stream the service no longer reads. A seek handle kept past the shutdown answers the same way.

An admin endpoint beside the service publishes cancellations through a publisher taken from the broker. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_shutdown.rs use ruststream_kinesis::KinesisPublisher; use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// The service, and a publisher for the code beside it that publishes outside any handler, such /// as an admin endpoint. fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> (RustStream, KinesisPublisher) { let admin = broker.publisher(); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }); (app, admin) } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_shutdown.rs use ruststream_kinesis::KinesisPublisher; use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// The service, and a publisher for the code beside it that publishes outside any handler, such /// as an admin endpoint. fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> (RustStream, KinesisPublisher) { let admin = broker.publisher(); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Place).build()); }); (app, admin) }

A subscription opens once every shard it took has a reader and a starting cursor; a stream the service lacks fails startup unless the descriptor creates it. Each subscription opens in three steps. First the descriptor is checked before any request: an empty stream name or a shard count below one fails startup with KinesisError::Invalid. Then one DescribeStreamSummary asks the service for the stream. A stream it does not have fails startup with KinesisError::Stream, which names the stream, so a mistyped name stops the service before it reads anything. Last, the subscription lists the stream's shards, takes a lease on each shard it can, and opens a reader with its starting cursor on each one. The subscription is open when that first pass is done. From that moment every record published to the stream reaches it. A shard another instance holds is left to that instance, and the subscription takes it later if its lease lapses. A failure inside the first pass, such as a lease store that does not answer, reaches the subscription's stream after startup and is logged there. One broker reads a stream through one subscription. A second subscription of the same broker to a stream it already reads is refused when it opens.

The stream payouts is the platform team's, and the service never creates it. On a stand without that stream, the service stops at startup. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_broker_startup.rs /// Pays out a settled order. The stream `payouts` is the platform team's: the service reads it /// and never creates it. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("payouts"))] async fn pay(payout: &Payout) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payout.order, payout.cents, "payout sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(pay); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_broker_startup.rs /// Pays out a settled order. The stream `payouts` is the platform team's: the service reads it /// and never creates it. struct Pay; impl Handle<Payout> for Pay { fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payout.order, payout.cents, "payout sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("payouts"), Pay).build()); }) }

Context<'_, KinesisContext> gives a handler the record's position and the seek handle, through the Position and SeekHandle keys. The subscription builds a KinesisContext once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers. Building it costs three reference-count increments: the shard id and the sequence number are shared with the delivery, and the seeker is the subscription's own. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is one of the two keys: Key Value What it is Position KinesisPosition the record's own place: its shard and its sequence number, as KinesisPosition::Sequence SeekHandle KinesisSeeker the handle that moves the subscription Both keys are in the prelude. A body that reads both takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per field, as the manual form does. A key the context does not carry is a compile error, not a lookup that finds nothing. A batch handler has a context of its own, with the seek handle only.

The handler writes where each order sits in the stream to an audit trail. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_context.rs /// Writes where each order sits in the stream to the audit trail. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn audit( order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>, Out(trail): Out<impl Publisher, Trail>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { // A delivered record's position is always one record of one shard. let KinesisPosition::Sequence { shard, sequence } = at else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; tracing::info!(order.id, shard, sequence, "order located"); let located = Located { order: order.id, shard, sequence, }; if trail.message(&located).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_context.rs /// Writes where each order sits in the stream to the audit trail. struct Audit; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>, KinesisContext> for Audit where Entry: OutEntry<Trail, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { // A delivered record's position is always one record of one shard. let KinesisPosition::Sequence { shard, sequence } = ctx.context(Position) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; tracing::info!(order.id, shard, sequence, "order located"); let located = Located { order: order.id, shard, sequence, }; outs.get(Trail) .message(&located) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

A batch handler's context, KinesisBatchContext, carries only the seek handle, so asking for a record's position in a batch body does not compile. A batch spans many records, often from several shards, so it has no single position. The subscription builds the context once per batch from its first record, and it holds what every record of the batch shares: the SeekHandle key, the same key a KinesisContext carries. A batch body takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisBatchContext> and reads the handle with ctx.context(SeekHandle). A seek from a batch body moves the whole subscription, so the next batch reads from the new position. Ctx<Position> in a batch body is a compile error.

The handler drains jobs two at a time, and a batch that holds the marker job moves the subscription to the tip. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_context_batch.rs /// Drains jobs a batch at a time; a batch holding the marker job moves the subscription to the /// tip, so the backlog behind it is skipped. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("jobs"))] async fn drain(jobs: &[Job], ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisBatchContext>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs drained"); if jobs.iter().any(|job| job.id == MARKER) && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::latest()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_context_batch.rs /// Drains jobs a batch at a time; a batch holding the marker job moves the subscription to the /// tip, so the backlog behind it is skipped. struct Drain; impl Handle<[Job], (), (), KinesisBatchContext> for Drain { async fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisBatchContext>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs drained"); if !jobs.iter().any(|job| job.id == MARKER) { return Ok(()); } ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::latest()) .await .map_err(|_| jobs.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()) } }

User headers ride an RSK2 envelope in front of the payload, only when there are any; a record from another producer reads as headerless. A Kinesis record carries a data blob and a partition key and nothing else. So the publisher writes the headers a message carries into a small envelope in front of the payload. The partition key stays out of it: it travels in the record's own partition-key field. A record with no other headers is the plain payload, which any Kinesis consumer reads as it is. The envelope is the four bytes RSK2, a big-endian u32 length of the header block, the header block, and then the payload. The block holds each header as a big-endian u32 name length, the name, a big-endian u32 value length and the value. So a value comes back byte for byte, whatever bytes it holds. Records written by earlier releases in the RSK1 text envelope still read back with their headers. A record without the magic, or whose header block does not parse, reads as a payload with no headers, so a record from another producer reaches the handler as that producer wrote it. A record aggregated by the Kinesis Producer Library packs many user records into one. The subscription reports it as KinesisError::AggregatedRecord, which the runtime logs, and moves on: the record is never handed to a handler, and the shard's checkpoint moves past it.

A payment's signature, raw bytes no text header could carry, travels in the envelope and reaches the handler unchanged. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_context_envelope.rs /// Accepts a payment that carries its signature, the raw bytes of the producer's MAC, in the /// `x-signature` header; an unsigned one is dropped. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("payments"))] async fn verify( payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Some(signature) = ctx.headers().get("x-signature") else { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "unsigned payment dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let verified = Verified { payment: payment.id, signature: signature.to_vec(), }; if ledger.message(&verified).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_context_envelope.rs /// Accepts a payment that carries its signature, the raw bytes of the producer's MAC, in the /// `x-signature` header; an unsigned one is dropped. struct Verify; impl<Entry> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Verify where Entry: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Some(signature) = ctx.headers().get("x-signature") else { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "unsigned payment dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let verified = Verified { payment: payment.id, signature: signature.to_vec(), }; outs.get(Ledger) .message(&verified) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

Every delivery carries its sequence number, its shard and its partition key as headers, where the framework's per-key dispatch finds the key. Header Constant Value kinesis-sequence-number SEQUENCE_HEADER the record's sequence number on its shard, a decimal string too wide for an integer kinesis-shard-id SHARD_HEADER the shard the record was read from, such as shardId-000000000000 partition-key PARTITION_KEY_HEADER the record's partition key The subscription writes the three headers from the record's own fields, next to the headers the producer wrote in the envelope. A handler reads them from ctx.headers(), as text with get_str. The sequence number and the shard name the same record that the Position key names. The partition key under partition-key is the key the core's IncomingMessage::partition_key reports. So workers(n, by_key) runs the records of one key one after another on one lane, in the order the shard holds them, while records of other keys run beside them. A retry copy carries the delivery's headers, so it keeps the record's partition key.

The meter is each reading's partition key, so the readings of one meter are billed in order on four lanes. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_context_headers.rs use ruststream_kinesis::{PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, SEQUENCE_HEADER, SHARD_HEADER}; /// Bills each meter reading. The meter is the record's partition key, so the readings of one /// meter run one after another on four lanes, and in the order the stream holds them. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("meters"), workers(4, by_key))] async fn bill( reading: &Reading, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(bills): Out<impl Publisher, Bills>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let headers = ctx.headers(); let (Some(meter), Some(shard), Some(sequence)) = ( headers.get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER), headers.get_str(SHARD_HEADER), headers.get_str(SEQUENCE_HEADER), ) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; tracing::info!(meter, shard, sequence, reading.kwh, "reading billed"); let charge = Bill { meter: meter.to_owned(), kwh: reading.kwh, }; if bills.message(&charge).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_context_headers.rs use ruststream_kinesis::{PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, SEQUENCE_HEADER, SHARD_HEADER}; /// Bills each meter reading. The meter is the record's partition key, so the readings of one /// meter run one after another on four lanes, and in the order the stream holds them. struct Charge; impl<Entry> Handle<Reading, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Charge where Entry: OutEntry<Bills, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let headers = ctx.headers(); let (Some(meter), Some(shard), Some(sequence)) = ( headers.get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER), headers.get_str(SHARD_HEADER), headers.get_str(SEQUENCE_HEADER), ) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; tracing::info!(meter, shard, sequence, reading.kwh, "reading billed"); let bill = Bill { meter: meter.to_owned(), kwh: reading.kwh, }; outs.get(Bills) .message(&bill) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("meters"), Charge) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ) .out(Bills, Publish::default()) .build(); }) }

A LeaseStore holds each shard's owner and checkpoint: acquire, renew, checkpoint, read and release, with SHARD_END marking a finished shard. Kinesis keeps no record of who reads a shard or how far a reader got, so the subscription keeps both in a store. KinesisBroker::lease_store installs one, and every subscription of the broker uses it. Without the call the broker uses a MemoryLeaseStore, correct for one instance of a service. Several instances share the shards through a store they all reach, such as DynamoLeaseStore. A subscription acquires a shard for its instance before it reads it, and a shard another live instance holds is left to that instance. A lease lasts ten seconds, and the reader renews it every three. A failed renewal means another instance has taken the shard, and the reader stops at once without writing a checkpoint. An expired lease is free to take, so the shards of an instance that stopped move to the others. Every acknowledgement that moves a shard's checkpoint is one checkpoint call, accepted only while the instance holds the lease. A reader starts at the checkpoint the store reads back as LeaseState, and at the tip when there is none. A shard read to its end is checkpointed as SHARD_END, which lets its children start, and then released. A reader that stops also releases its shard, so the next owner need not wait for the lease to expire. Each call names the shard by its LeaseKey, so one store serves every stream of a broker. A store that fails a call reports a LeaseError; the subscription reports it as KinesisError::Lease naming the stream and the shard, and tries the shard again at its next listing. The in-process transport of a TestApp test consults no store.

The service takes its store from the code that starts it; two instances on one store split the shards of inventory. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_leases_store.rs /// Applies each stock change. Every instance of the service runs this handler; the lease store /// decides which instance reads which shard. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("inventory"))] async fn apply(change: &StockChange) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.delta, "stock changed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, leases: Arc<dyn LeaseStore>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(leases), |b| { b.include(apply); }, ) } examples/manual/kinesis_leases_store.rs /// Applies each stock change. Every instance of the service runs this handler; the lease store /// decides which instance reads which shard. struct Apply; impl Handle<StockChange> for Apply { fn handle( &self, change: &StockChange, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.delta, "stock changed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, leases: Arc<dyn LeaseStore>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(leases), |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("inventory"), Apply).build()); }, ) }

DynamoLeaseStore keeps leases in a DynamoDB table, so several instances share the shards; the table needs only a string key lease_key. It needs the dynamodb-lease feature of the crate. DynamoLeaseStore::new takes the AWS configuration and the table name. The table has a string partition key named lease_key and nothing else; on-demand billing fits it. One row holds one shard of one stream, under the key stream:shard, so one table serves every stream of a service. The row holds the owner, the lease's expiry, the checkpoint and a counter bumped on every write. Every write is conditional, so two instances never both hold a shard, and a checkpoint lands only while its writer holds the lease. The checkpoints outlive the process, so a restarted instance resumes each shard where its acknowledgements stopped. The broker is built from the same configuration with KinesisBroker::from_config, so both reach one account and region. The service's credentials need dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:UpdateItem on the table. Each instance needs an owner id of its own; a table written by an earlier version of this crate is read through legacy_stream.

LeaseKey names one shard of one stream; a store of your own keys its rows by the key's stream:shard form. Every LeaseStore call names its shard by a LeaseKey. The stream is the name the subscription's KinesisStream was given, and the shard is the id the service assigned. Shard ids repeat across streams, so a store keys by both, and one store serves every stream of a broker. LeaseKey displays as stream:shard; a stream name holds no colon, so the form is unambiguous, and a store that keeps one string key writes it. A store of your own implements the five methods of LeaseStore and is installed with KinesisBroker::lease_store. A store for one instance grants every lease; a store for several instances makes acquire, renew and checkpoint conditional on the owner, as DynamoLeaseStore does.

A store for one instance keeps its checkpoints in a map keyed by the key's string form. examples/kinesis_leases_key.rs /// Checkpoints in a string-keyed map, for a single instance that owns every shard. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Checkpoints(Mutex<HashMap<String, String>>); impl LeaseStore for Checkpoints { fn checkpoint<'a>( &'a self, key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, sequence: &'a str, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async move { self.0 .lock() .map_err(|err| err.to_string())? .insert(key.to_string(), sequence.to_owned()); Ok(true) }) } fn read<'a>(&'a self, key: &'a LeaseKey) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<LeaseState, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async move { let checkpoint = self .0 .lock() .map_err(|err| err.to_string())? .get(&key.to_string()) .cloned(); let mut state = LeaseState::default(); state.checkpoint = checkpoint; Ok(state) }) } // One instance owns every shard, so a lease is always granted and never lapses. fn acquire<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, _ttl: Duration, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(true) }) } fn renew<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, _ttl: Duration, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(true) }) } fn release<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<(), LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(()) }) } } The service installs it on its broker. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_leases_key.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, checkpoints: Arc<Checkpoints>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("loyalty", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(checkpoints), |b| { b.include(credit); }, ) } examples/manual/kinesis_leases_key.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, checkpoints: Arc<Checkpoints>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("loyalty", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(checkpoints), |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("loyalty"), Credit).build()); }, ) }

legacy_stream names the stream a table's bare shard rows belong to, so a table written by an earlier version resumes from them. Earlier versions of this crate keyed a row by the shard id alone, such as shardId-000000000000. A bare row names no stream, and every stream's first shard has that id. So DynamoLeaseStore reads a bare row only for the stream legacy_stream names. A shard of that stream with no checkpoint under its own stream:shard row resumes from its bare row, and the first read copies the checkpoint to the new row. A checkpoint already on the new row wins over the bare one. Other streams ignore the bare rows. Without legacy_stream, a shard whose bare row holds a checkpoint is refused with a lease error that names the table, the shard and the stream, and it is not read until the stream is named or the row is deleted. Once the upgraded service has opened a subscription on every stream it reads, every bare row with progress has its copy; the rows whose lease_key holds no : can then be deleted, and the setting dropped. A table that served several streams before the upgrade holds, in each bare row, the checkpoint of whichever stream wrote last. No stream can resume from such a row: delete the bare rows and open each stream with start_at at the position it should read from. The two versions lease different rows, so an old and a new instance can read one shard at once; stop the old instances before the new ones start.

The table returns-leases served the stream returns alone before the upgrade. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_leases_legacy.rs /// The table was written by an earlier version for the stream `returns` alone, so its bare rows /// are that stream's progress. fn broker(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> KinesisBroker { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table).legacy_stream("returns")); KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases) } examples/manual/kinesis_leases_legacy.rs /// The table was written by an earlier version for the stream `returns` alone, so its bare rows /// are that stream's progress. fn broker(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> KinesisBroker { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table).legacy_stream("returns")); KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases) }

MemoryLeaseStore is the default store: correct for one service instance, and empty again after a restart. A broker that names no lease store creates one with MemoryLeaseStore::new. It keeps leases and checkpoints in the memory of the process, so one instance reads every shard of its streams and orders a split's children after their parents. Brokers of one process that share it through an Arc share its leases and checkpoints. A new process starts with an empty store. So a restarted service opens each shard at the tip, unless start_at names another position. The records published while the service was down are not read, and a held record does not come back. A service that must resume where it stopped, or runs in more than one instance, uses a store outside the process, such as DynamoLeaseStore.

owner_id names this instance in the lease table; left out, each broker takes an id of its own, unique to that broker. A lease store records which owner holds each shard, and grants an owner the leases it already holds. So an instance that restarts under the same id takes its shards back at once, without waiting for its old leases to expire. A stable name per instance, such as a pod name, gives that. A fixed id must never be shared by two instances that run at the same time: both would hold the same shards, and each would read them. The DynamoLeaseStore table shows the id in the lease_owner column of each row, which tells an operator which instance reads which shard.

The dispatch service names each instance after its host.
